movedToNotes: Plan: Basic Plan for Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth in Seoul (10 years)
2005 baseline: 52.34 Mt CO₂e (million tons of all greenhouse gases, converted into the amount of CO₂ that warms the same)
Half by 2033, net zero by 2050

Vehicle grades 1 to 5: Korea's emission grades, 5 pollutes most
Green transport zones = central Seoul areas where the city limits polluting cars
Combustion engine = any gas or diesel engine
Slow down on 2035. Say: "By 2035, Seoul plans to ban gas and diesel cars from central Seoul."

headline: One Less Nuclear Power Plant

elements.old: Eco-Mileage — voluntary, rewarded, and the single most effective measure
elements.new: Eco-Mileage rewards · 1.68 million participants · 190,000 TOE saved

elements.old: Target met June 2014 — six months early
elements.new: Goal reached June 2014 · six months early
of the goal from using less energy

elements.old: “A city government decided its job was to reduce demand. Utilities get paid to sell more.”
elements.new: Electricity made in Seoul: from under 3% in 2011 to about 5% in Phase 2

movedToNotes: Why it started: launched 2012 after Fukushima (2011) and a 2011 Seoul blackout
Goal: save or produce 2 million TOE, about one nuclear reactor's yearly output
TOE = ton of oil equivalent, a unit for comparing kinds of energy

Eco-Mileage: 1.68 million participants by June 2014, saved 190,000 TOE. It was the most effective single measure in Phase 1. People could see and compare their energy use and earned small rewards. Say the 1.68 million out loud, because it comes back on the last slide.
79/21 is the planned split of the 2M goal: 1.59 million TOE from saving energy, 410,000 TOE from new renewables (exactly 79.5 and 20.5%). Sources give no split for the final 2.04M.
Phase 2: 4.65 million TOE saved 2012 to 2017 (C40, a network of big cities on climate)
Electricity made in Seoul: 2.9% in 2011 to 5% (C40) or 5.5% by 2015 (city figure), so say about 5%
Legacy: Seoul Energy Corporation was set up to carry the work forward
Say: "Seoul decided its job was to cut how much energy the city uses."
Next: making power, with solar

headline: Solar Panels on Balconies

elements.old: Typical Seoul apartment slab — mini-PV mounted on every balcony railing
elements.new: Seoul apartment block · small solar panels on balcony railings
SOLAR CITY SEOUL · PROGRESS TOWARD 1 GW

elements.old: Not enough installable surface area. The same wall NYC hits.
elements.new: Not enough space for panels on buildings and public facilities

movedToNotes: Seoul treats the balcony railing as a place to make electricity
Solar City Seoul started in 2017. Goals: 1 GW more solar by 2022 and solar for 1 million households. Budget about ₩1.7 trillion (the US$1.46 billion on the slide).
Kits: standard, subsidized, renters can install them, with published design and safety standards
In 2019 the program was reported as ahead of schedule.
MW = megawatt, GW = gigawatt. 1 GW = 1,000 MW, so 357.1 MW is about a third of the goal.
Seoul was the first Korean city to pay small solar plants (50 kW and under) for each kWh they make, for five years (a 2013 measure)
In New York the barriers are the building code, permits and landlord consent.
Next: a dense, tall city has little roof per apartment, so saving energy in existing buildings matters too

headline: Paying for Building Retrofits

elements.old: Retrofit by loan, not by fine.
The city hands you the money.
elements.new: Open to homes, hospitals and universities

elements.old: interest, up to 100% of facility cost
elements.new: a year · loans up to 100% of eligible cost

elements.old: target — 20% of stock over 20 years old
elements.new: 20% of Seoul's buildings that are over 20 years old

elements.old: per ton over the cap, per year
elements.new: per ton of CO₂e over the limit, each year
Goal: 40% cut by 2030 · 80% by 2050, from 2005 levels

elements.old: Seoul has the carrot and a weak stick. New York has the stick and no carrot. Neither half works alone.
elements.new: LL97 buildings over the limit: about 11% (2024 to 2029 limits) · about 63% (2030 limits, if nothing changes)

movedToNotes: Seoul: low-interest city loans for upgrades · New York: limits and fines, owners find the money
BRP history: started 2008. In 2012 it grew under One Less Nuclear Power Plant and opened to private universities, hospitals, then homes.
2013 changes: interest cut from 2.5% to 1.75% a year, and loans raised from 80% to 100% of the eligible cost
Results differ by source, so name the source
C40: 25,841 tons of CO₂ saved, about 4,200 projects, 2012 to 2015
Other C40 reporting: 72,000 buildings improved
SMG (Seoul city government): 20,000 buildings and houses, 192,234 TOE saved
100-building sample (2012 to 2013): homes used 10% less energy, other buildings 6.5% less
59 welfare facilities (social service buildings) retrofitted: about 15% less energy
Buildings = 56% of Seoul's energy use (emissions share is about two-thirds)
LL97 targets are counted from 2005 levels, and the limits tighten a lot in 2030: offices by 64.5% and multifamily by 50.4% compared with 2024 to 2029
Say: "My second recommendation at the end is a city loan fund for LL97 upgrades, on terms like Seoul's."
